examples.label: aⁿbⁿ
examples.purpose: Each failed alternative is undone at once; nothing deeper is revisited.

examples.label: Wrong first guess
examples.purpose: A takes one a, then b fails, and the parser backs into A for its second way.

examples.label: Palindromes
examples.purpose: Guessing the middle: lookahead cannot tell where a palindrome turns, so each position is tried.

examples.label: Dangling else
examples.purpose: The longer alternative goes first, so else binds to the nearest if; the shared prefix is matched again after a failure.
text: S -> if c then S else S | if c then S | x
strings: if c then if c then x else x
if c then x else x

examples.label: Shortest alternative first
examples.purpose: With ordered choice A stops after one a and the rest fails. Complete search accepts; so does reordering the alternatives.

examples.label: Longest alternative first
examples.purpose: The same language with the alternatives swapped: ordered choice accepts, since the long way is tried first.

examples.label: Tiny statement language
examples.purpose: A keyword selects the alternative, as in real recursive-descent parsers. id and num stand for names and numbers.
text: Stmt -> id = Expr ; | print Expr ; | while ( Expr ) Block | if ( Expr ) Block Else
Expr' -> + Term Expr' | - Term Expr' | eps
strings: while ( id ) { print id ; id = id - num ; }
if ( id ) { id = num ; } else { id = num ; }

examples.label: Assignment or call
examples.purpose: Both start with id: the parser tries assignment, backs up one token and tries the call. One more token of lookahead avoids it.
strings: id = id + num ; id ( id , num ) ;

examples.label: Regular expressions
examples.purpose: The regex language, LL-ready, parsed by recursive descent. Input such as (a|b)*abb needs no spaces.

examples.label: Sentences (running example)
examples.purpose: Every alternative starts with a different word, so no alternative is ever undone. old snores is rejected: the noun is missing.

examples.label: Left recursion
examples.purpose: E calls E at the same position without reading anything, so a top-down parser would loop forever. The run stops at the first repeat.

examples.label: Hidden left recursion
examples.purpose: S -> A S looks right-recursive, but A can be empty, so S still calls itself before reading anything.

examples.label: Left recursion removed
examples.purpose: The expression grammar with the recursion moved to the right: the parser terminates and seldom backtracks.

examples.label: Repeated work
examples.purpose: Both alternatives of E start with T, so a T that is not followed by + is matched twice; every nesting level doubles the work.

examples.label: Sentences with an adjective list (left-recursive)
examples.purpose: The adjective list calls itself before reading a word, so the run stops at the first repeat.
